# Aristotle, Rhetoric (trans. W. Rhys Roberts), Stakeholder-Engagement Distillation

**Source:** Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, translated by W. Rhys Roberts (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1924; The Works of Aristotle, vol. XI). Internet Classics Archive transcription, http://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/rhetoric.html. **Licence:** Public domain (translation published 1924; translator died 1929). **Scope:** open. Cited as `(Bk N, Part M)`; every quotation is Roberts's English.

## Stakeholder-Engagement Relevance

The *Rhetoric* is about speaking to people who decide. Its organising claim is that the hearer, not the speaker or the subject, *"determines the speech's end and object"* [V] (Bk I, Part 3), and it extends "judge" to anyone you must persuade: *"any one is your judge whom you have to persuade"* [V] (Bk II, Part 18). That is the stakeholder-engagement problem stated from the side of the person who has to bring others to a decision. The source supplies four things the axis uses. First, an account of credibility: hearers trust a speaker who shows good sense, good moral character and goodwill (Bk II, Part 1). Second, a working catalogue of the feelings that change how people judge (anger and calm, friendliness and enmity, fear and confidence, shame, kindness, pity, indignation, envy, emulation), each analysed by state of mind, towards whom, and on what grounds (Bk II, Parts 1–11). Third, an account of audiences: character by age and fortune, and the interests built into each form of government (Bk I, Part 8; Bk II, Parts 12–17). Fourth, the mechanics of a case put to others: stating the aim, removing prejudice, narrating, answering the other side, and closing (Bk III, Parts 13–19).

The source is a persuader's manual, and it says plainly that many of its devices work on hearers' defects. The author holds that a case should fairly be fought *"with no help beyond the bare facts"* [V] (Bk III, Part 1), that the speaker *"must not make people believe what is wrong"* [V] (Bk I, Part 1), and that arguing both sides is for seeing the facts and answering unfair argument (Bk I, Part 1). This distillation uses the emotional and audience material to understand stakeholders and to engage them honestly, and uses the catalogue of devices and spurious arguments mainly for recognising them when others use them. It does not use "stakeholder"; the source's parties are speakers, opponents, judges, assemblies and audiences. Every move from them to modern stakeholders is this distillation's.

## Key Concepts for Stakeholder-Engagement

1. <!-- concept: audience-determines-the-speech --> **The audience sets the purpose.** Of speaker, subject and person addressed, *"it is the last one, the hearer, that determines the speech's end and object"* [V]. Hearers who decide about the future make political oratory, aimed at the expedient; hearers who decide about the past, forensic, aimed at the just; observers who judge the speaker's skill, ceremonial, aimed at the honourable (Bk I, Part 3) [AR]. Each kind of speaker will often concede other points but holds firm on its own end: the litigant may admit harm, *"But that he is guilty of injustice he will never admit"* [V] (Bk I, Part 3). (Source: Aristotle, *Rhetoric*, Bk I, Part 3)

2. <!-- concept: three-modes-of-persuasion --> **Three things persuade.** *"The first kind depends on the personal character of the speaker; the second on putting the audience into a certain frame of mind; the third on the proof, or apparent proof, provided by the words of the speech itself."* [V] Character should be shown by what is said in the engagement, *"not by what people think of his character before he begins to speak"* [V] (Bk I, Part 2). (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk I, Part 2)

3. <!-- concept: good-sense-character-goodwill --> **Credibility has three parts.** Hearers trust a speaker *"apart from any proof"* [V] for *"good sense, good moral character, and goodwill"* [V] (Bk II, Part 1). The author derives the three from the ways advice goes wrong:

   > *"Men either form a false opinion through want of good sense; or they form a true opinion, but because of their moral badness do not say what they really think; or finally, they are both sensible and upright, but not well disposed to their hearers, and may fail in consequence to recommend what they know to be the best course."* [V] (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Part 1)

   A stakeholder who distrusts the convenor doubts one of these three; the remedy differs by which. (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Part 1)

4. <!-- concept: emotions-three-heads --> **Read each feeling three ways.** *"The Emotions are all those feelings that so change men as to affect their judgements, and that are also attended by pain or pleasure."* [V] Each is analysed by the state of mind of those who feel it, the people it is felt towards, and its grounds: *"unless we know all three, we shall be unable to arouse anger in any one"* [V] (Bk II, Part 1). The same three heads serve for understanding a feeling as for arousing it. (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Part 1)

5. <!-- concept: anger-and-calming --> **Anger comes from slights; calm from acknowledgement and time.** Anger is *"an impulse, accompanied by pain, to a conspicuous revenge for a conspicuous slight directed without justification towards what concerns oneself or towards what concerns one's friends"* [V] (Bk II, Part 2). Slights include contempt for what people care most about, not perceiving their needs, indifference to the pain one gives (*"this is why we get angry with bringers of bad news"* [V]) and forgetting: *"Forgetfulness, too, causes anger, as when our own names are forgotten, trifling as this may be"* [V] (Bk II, Part 2). Calm follows when the slight was involuntary, when people are taken seriously, and when the other side acknowledges fault (Bk II, Part 3) [AP]:

   > *"towards those who admit their fault and are sorry: since we accept their grief at what they have done as satisfaction, and cease to be angry."* [V] (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Part 3)

   The author's example of denial is the punishment of servants: those who deny an obvious offence are punished all the more, because *"it is shameless to deny what is obvious, and those who are shameless towards us slight us"* [V]. And *"time puts an end to anger"* [V] (Bk II, Part 3).

6. <!-- concept: friendly-feeling --> **Goodwill and enmity.** Friendly feeling is *"wishing for him what you believe to be good things, not for your own sake but for his, and being inclined, so far as you can, to bring these things about"* [V] (Bk II, Part 4). People feel friendly towards those who have treated them, or those they care for, well for their sake, *"those who are not too ready to show us our mistakes"* [V], those who do not nurse grudges, those *"who are honest with us, including those who will tell us of their own weak points"* [V], and those who do not frighten them; friendship is caused by kindnesses done unasked and not proclaimed (Bk II, Part 4) [AP]. Enmity differs: it can attach to a whole class, and *"anger can be cured by time; but hatred cannot"* [V] (Bk II, Part 4). (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Parts 2–4)

7. <!-- concept: shame-before-those-who-matter --> **Shame and the people who matter.** Shame is felt before *"those whose opinion of us matters to us"* [V], more when things are done openly (*"shame dwells in the eyes"* [V]), and differently with intimates and strangers: *"before the former of what seem genuine faults, before the latter of what seem conventional ones"* [V] (Bk II, Part 6). Fear, similarly, *"sets us thinking what can be done"* [V] only while some hope remains (Bk II, Part 5). (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Parts 5–6)

8. <!-- concept: audience-character --> **Know the audience's character and interests.** *"For all men are persuaded by considerations of their interest, and their interest lies in the maintenance of the established order."* [V] (Bk I, Part 8) Each form of government pursues its own end (freedom, wealth, education and national institutions, the tyrant's protection). Character also varies with age and fortune: the young trust readily and overdo everything, the old, formed for the most part of the contrary, are *"sure about nothing and under-do everything"* [V], those in their prime judge people correctly (Bk II, Parts 12–14) [AP]. *"People always think well of speeches adapted to, and reflecting, their own character"* [V] (Bk II, Part 13). (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk I, Part 8; Bk II, Parts 12–17)

9. <!-- concept: maxims --> **Start from what people already hold.** Arguments should start from opinions *"accepted by our judges or by those whose authority they recognize"* [V] (Bk II, Part 22). Hearers *"love to hear him succeed in expressing as a universal truth the opinions which they hold themselves about particular cases"* [V], so the speaker must find out what views they already hold (Bk II, Part 21) [AR]; maxims also display the speaker's moral principles (Bk II, Part 21). Facts specific to the case beat commonplaces that would fit any case (Bk II, Part 22) [AR]. (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Parts 21–22)

10. <!-- concept: dispelling-prejudice --> **Meeting prejudice and calumny.** A defendant removes prejudice at the start, and a prosecutor excites it at the close (Bk III, Part 14) [AR]. The ways to meet it include denying the fact, the harm, its size, the wrong or the disgrace; admitting harm but not wrong (*"Thus Iphicrates replying to Nausicrates, admitted that he had done the deed alleged, and that he had done Nausicrates harm, but not that he had done him wrong."* [V]); and pleading *"mistake, or bad luck, or necessity"* [V] (Bk III, Part 15). Calumny can itself be denounced, showing *"that it raises false issues, and that it means a lack of confidence in the merits of his case"* [V] (Bk III, Part 15). (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk III, Parts 14–15)

11. <!-- concept: introduction-shows-aim --> **Say what the engagement is for, then make the case.** *"A speech has two parts. You must state your case, and you must prove it."* [V] (Bk III, Part 13) The introduction's essential function is *"to show what the aim of the speech is"* [V], because *"Anything vague puzzles them"* [V] (Bk III, Part 14). Introductions *"are addressed not to ideal hearers, but to hearers as we find them"* [V], and introductions are popular with those *"whose case is weak, or looks weak"* [V] (Bk III, Part 14). The close should *"state what you have said and why you have said it"* [V] (Bk III, Part 19). (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk III, Parts 13–14, 19)

12. <!-- concept: equity --> **Equity and arbitration.** Equity is *"the sort of justice which goes beyond the written law"* [V]; among its rules: *"to settle a dispute by negotiation and not by force; to prefer arbitration to motion-for an arbitrator goes by the equity of a case, a judge by the strict law"* [V] (Bk I, Part 13). It also bids us look at intentions over actions and at *"the whole story"* [V] over the detail (Bk I, Part 13). (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk I, Part 13)

## Questions to Ask During Stakeholder-Engagement

The questions are this distillation's; the third column names the passage each one leans on.

### Phase 1: Mapping

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Find who decides | Which parties actually decide or must accept this, and which are observers? Anyone we must persuade counts. | Bk I, Part 3; Bk II, Part 18 |
| Find each party's end | Does each party judge mainly by expedience (future), by fairness about the past, or by honour and standing? | Bk I, Part 3 |
| Map interests in the status quo | What arrangement does each party's interest depend on, and what would change threaten? | Bk I, Part 8 |
| Read the audience's character | What are these parties like by age, experience, wealth and power: quick to trust or slow, sure of themselves or doubtful? | Bk II, Parts 12–17 |
| Check what they already believe | What views do they already hold about this, in their own words? | Bk II, Parts 21–22 |

### Phase 2: Framing the question

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| State the aim | Can we say in a sentence what this engagement is for, so nobody is left in suspense? | Bk III, Part 14 |
| Separate statement from case | Have we stated the question before arguing for an answer? | Bk III, Part 13 |
| Clear prejudice early | Is there a rumour or prior grievance about us that needs addressing at the start rather than the end? | Bk III, Parts 14–15 |
| Start from accepted ground | Which opinions do these parties already accept, and are we starting there rather than from our own premises? | Bk II, Part 22 |
| Use their facts | Which facts are specific to this situation and these parties, rather than general arguments that would fit anywhere? | Bk II, Part 22 |

### Phase 3: Convening

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Earn credibility in the room | What will show good sense, good character and goodwill in what we say here, rather than relying on our reputation beforehand? | Bk I, Part 2; Bk II, Part 1 |
| Prevent avoidable slights | Have we used people's names, acknowledged their particular situation, and taken their concerns seriously? | Bk II, Parts 2–3 |
| Hear them as they are | Are we speaking to these people as they are, or to an ideal audience? | Bk III, Part 14 |
| Fit style to setting | Is this a large meeting where broad strokes work, or a small one where detail and plain argument matter more? | Bk III, Part 12 |

### Phase 4: Surfacing conflict

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Locate the slight | Where anger appears: what does this party feel was slighted, and was it something they care about most? | Bk II, Part 2 |
| Anger or enmity | Is this anger at something we did, which acknowledgement and time can cure, or hostility to a whole class of people like us, which time does not cure? | Bk II, Part 4 |
| Name the real dispute | Is the disagreement about whether something happened, whether it did harm, how much, or whether it was justified? | Bk III, Part 17 |
| Separate harm from wrong | Can we admit the harm we caused without conceding a wrong we did not do, and say so plainly? | Bk III, Part 15 |
| Spot false issues | Is a calumny or a vivid story raising issues that are not the issue? | Bk III, Part 15; Bk II, Part 24 |
| Check public and private positions | What do parties approve of openly, and what would they choose in private? | Bk II, Part 23 (line 15) |

### Phase 5: Reaching agreement

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Acknowledge fault | Where we were at fault, have we said so and shown we regret it, rather than denying the obvious? | Bk II, Part 3 |
| Prefer negotiation | Can this be settled by negotiation or an arbitrator's sense of fairness rather than by strict rule or force? | Bk I, Part 13 |
| Look at the whole story | Are we judging parties by their intentions and their whole record, or by one detail? | Bk I, Part 13 |
| Make room for our proposal | If another proposal has been well received, have we answered it before putting ours? | Bk III, Part 17 |
| Answer by distinction | When asked a loaded or ambiguous question, are we answering with a fair distinction rather than a curt yes or no? | Bk III, Part 18 |

### Phase 6: Ratifying

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Recap what was agreed and why | Have we stated what was agreed and why, so the point decided is plain? | Bk III, Part 19 |
| Show we did what we said | Have we shown that we did what we undertook to do in this engagement? | Bk III, Part 19 |
| Express it in their terms | Is the agreement stated in terms that reflect the parties' own character and views? | Bk II, Part 13; Bk II, Part 21 |

### Phase 7: Post-engagement

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Keep goodwill | Are we doing kindnesses unasked and without announcing them, and being honest about our own weak points? | Bk II, Part 4 |
| Let anger settle | Where anger remains, have we left time and acknowledged fault, rather than pressing for a resolution now? | Bk II, Part 3 |
| Review fairly | In reviewing what went wrong, are we sorting misfortune and error of judgement from deliberate wrong, and avoiding hindsight about what would have been better? | Bk I, Part 13; Bk II, Part 23 (line 25) |

## What to Look For

**Signal:** A group that was calm becomes angry over something small: a name misspelled, a meeting moved without notice, a question unanswered.
**Diagnosis:** A slight. The author lists forgetting names, indifference to the pain one gives, and contempt for the things people most care about among the causes of anger (Bk II, Part 2) [AP].
**Follow-up:** Acknowledge it directly and treat the concern seriously; the author's account of calm is that people stop being angry with those who admit their fault and are sorry, and with those who are serious when they are serious (Bk II, Part 3).

**Signal:** Every argument is well made and nobody moves.
**Diagnosis:** The proof is present but the other two modes of persuasion are missing: the parties doubt the convenor's good sense, character or goodwill, or are in a frame of mind that turns the facts against the proposal (Bk I, Part 2; Bk II, Part 1) [AP].
**Follow-up:** Ask which of good sense, character or goodwill they doubt, and address that before restating the argument.

**Signal:** A rumour about the project ("they've already decided") shapes every meeting.
**Diagnosis:** Prejudice, which the source says a defendant must clear away first (Bk III, Part 14) [AP].
**Follow-up:** Address it at the opening of the next engagement: deny what is false, admit what is true, and show what the rumour gets wrong (Bk III, Part 15).

**Signal:** A party insists on being heard about a past grievance before discussing the future proposal.
**Diagnosis:** The party is judging as about the past (justice), while the convenor speaks about the future (expedience) (Bk I, Part 3) [AP].
**Follow-up:** Treat the grievance on its own terms first; separate what happened, whether it did harm, how much, and whether it was justified (Bk III, Part 17).

**Signal:** The engagement lead's presentation is polished and the room grows suspicious.
**Diagnosis:** Artificiality: the source holds that *"Naturalness is persuasive, artificiality is the contrary; for our hearers are prejudiced and think we have some design against them"* [V] (Bk III, Part 2).
**Follow-up:** Use the parties' ordinary words, fewer devices, and plain statements of what is proposed and why.

**Signal:** Hostility is directed at "management" or "the council" as a class, not at anything specific.
**Diagnosis:** Enmity rather than anger: directed at a class, and not cured by time as anger is (Bk II, Part 4) [AP].
**Follow-up:** Do not expect one acknowledgement to settle it; build goodwill over time through the conduct the author lists as producing friendly feeling (Bk II, Part 4).

## When to Use This Reference

- **Preparing to engage a group that must decide or accept something.** The audience analysis (what each party judges by, its interests in the status quo, its character) and the three sources of credibility give a structured way to prepare.
- **Strong feelings are running in the engagement.** The Book II catalogue says, for each feeling, what state of mind produces it, towards whom, and on what grounds, which is the information needed to understand it and to calm it.
- **The engagement carries a history of grievance or rumour.** Book III, Parts 14–15 on prejudice and calumny, and Book II, Part 3 on calm, give the moves.
- **Opening and closing an engagement.** The introduction's job (state the aim), the statement-then-argument structure, and the epilogue's recap (what was said and why) apply directly.
- **Recognising manipulation by others.** The spurious-argument catalogue (Bk II, Part 24) and the author's own remarks on devices that work on hearers' defects help a practitioner name what is being done in the room.
- Reach for OpenStax *Business Ethics* for who has standing as a stakeholder; the *Rhetoric* assumes the audience is given.
- Reach for OpenStax *Organizational Behavior* for negotiation and conflict as studied empirically; the *Rhetoric* describes feelings in the author's own account, not from studies.
- Reach for Liberating Structures for how to run the room, and the FLO Facilitation Guide when the engagement runs as a facilitated online course; the *Rhetoric* is written for a single speaker addressing hearers, not for facilitated dialogue.

## Worked Example

*The scenario is operator-authored; its events and outcome are the scenario's. The* Rhetoric *addresses speakers before assemblies, courts and ceremonies; carrying it to a modern public engagement is this distillation's move.*

A university library plans to move half its print collection to an off-site store to make room for study space. Three groups must accept the plan: senior faculty, students, and the family whose donation built the reading room. Word has already spread that "the library is getting rid of books".

**Mapping (Phase 1).** The librarian, Ruth, maps each group by what it judges by (Bk I, Part 3). Students judge by the future: will the change give them space? Senior faculty judge by the past: was the 2019 reorganisation, which lost material, handled fairly? The family judges by honour: is the reading room's name respected? She notes the source's sketch of elderly men, formed for the most part of the contrary of the young, who *"are sure about nothing and under-do everything"* [V] (Bk II, Part 13), and expects faculty doubt rather than enthusiasm.

**Framing (Phase 2).** Ruth opens the first faculty meeting by dealing with the rumour first, as the source advises a speaker facing prejudice to clear it away at the outset (Bk III, Part 14). She states what is true (half the print collection will move), what is false (nothing will be discarded), and the aim of the meeting in one sentence, because *"Anything vague puzzles them: so give them a grasp of the beginning, and they can hold fast to it and follow the argument"* [V] (Bk III, Part 14).

**Surfacing conflict (Phase 4).** A senior professor is angry: in 2019 his department's special collection was boxed without notice and some of it was lost. Ruth reads it through the source's account of anger as a response to a slight against what people care about most (Bk II, Part 2), and separates the questions the source separates: did it happen, did it do harm, how much, was it justified (Bk III, Part 17). It happened, it did harm, and it was not justified. She says so:

> *"towards those who admit their fault and are sorry: since we accept their grief at what they have done as satisfaction, and cease to be angry."* [V] (Source: *Rhetoric*, Bk II, Part 3)

**Reaching agreement (Phase 5).** Ruth proposes that each department name what must stay on site, and that disputes about individual items go to a small panel of faculty and librarians rather than to a library rule, following the source's preference for settling disputes by negotiation and preferring arbitration to strict law (Bk I, Part 13). With the family, she asks what the reading room stands for in their view, and the plan keeps the room's books and adds a plaque on the new study space.

**Ratifying and post-engagement (Phases 6–7).** At the closing meeting she states what was agreed and why, the recap the source gives to the epilogue (Bk III, Part 19). In the scenario, the move goes ahead with the professor on the panel.

What the example takes from the *Rhetoric*: the three judgements by which audiences decide (Bk I, Part 3); character by age (Bk II, Part 13); clearing prejudice first and stating the aim (Bk III, Part 14); anger as a response to a slight and calm through acknowledged fault (Bk II, Parts 2–3); the four issues in dispute (Bk III, Part 17); negotiation and arbitration (Bk I, Part 13); the recap (Bk III, Part 19). The library, the groups and the outcome are the scenario's.

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **Treating the emotion catalogue as a toolkit for manipulation.** *Signal:* plans to "make them angry at the other side" or to frighten them into agreement. *Why it fails (the distillation's judgment, resting on the author's own statements):* the author calls moving the judge to anger, envy or pity like warping *"a carpenter's rule before using it"* [V], and says the speaker *"must not make people believe what is wrong"* [V] (Bk I, Part 1). *Instead:* use the analysis to understand the feelings in the room and to answer them honestly.
- **Arguing only the merits.** *Signal:* a strong case that does not land. *Why it fails:* the source names three modes of persuasion, and proof is only one; character and the hearers' frame of mind are the others (Bk I, Part 2). *Instead:* ask which of good sense, character and goodwill the parties doubt.
- **Denying the obvious.** *Signal:* the convenor defends a past failure everyone knows about. *Why it fails:* the source's example is servants, punished all the more for denying an obvious offence, because it is shameless to deny what is obvious, and shamelessness towards us is a slight (Bk II, Part 3); carrying it to a convenor is this distillation's move. *Instead:* admit the fault and the harm.
- **Ignoring the small slights.** *Signal:* names misspelled, questions unanswered, meetings rearranged without notice. *Why it fails:* the source lists forgetting names and indifference to the pain one gives among the causes of anger (Bk II, Part 2). *Instead:* treat these details as part of the engagement.
- **Long preambles.** *Signal:* the introduction runs longer than the proposal. *Why it fails:* the source says introductions are popular with those whose case is weak or looks weak, since it pays them to dwell on anything rather than the facts (Bk III, Part 14). *Instead:* state the aim, then the case.
- **The polished pitch.** *Signal:* rehearsed lines and slides that look designed to persuade. *Why it fails:* artificiality makes hearers suspect a design against them (Bk III, Part 2). *Instead:* speak in the parties' ordinary words.
- **Generic arguments.** *Signal:* the case for the proposal would fit any organisation. *Why it fails:* the source says special facts make an argument belong to this case and commonplaces make it fit any (Bk II, Part 22). *Instead:* build the case from facts specific to these parties.

## Integration with Other References

| Reference | Connection |
|---|---|
| OpenStax, *Business Ethics* | Carries what the *Rhetoric* lacks: who counts as a stakeholder and how to weigh their claims. The *Rhetoric* assumes its audience is given (an assembly, a court, a crowd) and supplies the account of how that audience judges. Use Business Ethics to decide whom to engage; use the *Rhetoric* to understand how each group will hear you. |
| OpenStax, *Organizational Behavior* | OB separates process conflict from relationship conflict and treats negotiation stages and cross-cultural negotiation styles. The *Rhetoric*'s anger-and-calm analysis gives the older, descriptive account of why conflict turns personal (a perceived slight) and what settles it (acknowledgement, seriousness, time). Use OB for the empirical frame; use the *Rhetoric* for the reading of a particular person's anger. |
| OpenStax, *Psychology 2e* | Presents the Yale attitude-change approach (source credibility and attractiveness; message subtlety, sidedness and timing; audience attention, intelligence, self-esteem and age) and the elaboration likelihood model's central and peripheral routes to persuasion (Ch 12.3). The *Rhetoric*'s three sources of a speaker's credibility and its account of hearers by age and fortune cover related ground in the author's own terms. Use *Psychology 2e* for the research framing; use the *Rhetoric* for the fuller account of how particular audiences judge. |
| U.S. Marine Corps, *MCDP 1: Warfighting* | MCDP 1's orienting discipline asks for understanding an opposing party on its own terms. The *Rhetoric*'s audience analysis (what each party judges by, its interests, its character by age and fortune) does similar work for any party, cooperative or not, but from the standpoint of persuading it rather than defeating it. |
| Liberating Structures; FLO Facilitation Guide | Liberating Structures carries practices for participatory meetings; FLO, for facilitating online learning. The *Rhetoric* is written for one speaker addressing hearers who decide; pair it with a facilitation source when the engagement needs dialogue rather than a case put to an audience. |

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The author refers to the *Topics*, *Analytics*, *Politics* and treatise on the *Art of Poetry* for fuller treatments; none is held in this corpus. He attributes lines of argument to earlier rhetoric manuals (Corax, Callippus, Pamphilus, and the Art before Theodorus) and cites Gorgias, Isocrates and Socrates; none is held. This distillation uses only the *Rhetoric*'s own statements.

**Named limits of the source.** The *Rhetoric* does not use the word *stakeholder* and offers no account of who has standing; its parties are speakers, opponents and the hearers who decide in assemblies, courts and ceremonies. Its account of emotions and of character by age and fortune is the author's description, not an empirical finding, and it includes the author's own judgements about groups such as the well-born and the newly rich (Bk II, Parts 9, 15–16). It openly includes devices that work on hearers' defects and arguments that only look valid; this distillation carries them for recognition, not for use. Every application to modern stakeholder engagement is the distillation's.

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Every `[V]` quotation is copied from a `[V]` passage in the deep reference `corpus.commons/demo/references/aristotle-rhetoric-deep.md`, and is Roberts's English exactly as the converted source prints it, including the hyphens it uses for dashes ("motion-for", "pity-one"). `[V]` here means the translator's words; Aristotle's Greek does not survive on the source. Passages the deep reference paraphrases are carried as `[AP]`, `[AR]` or `[AE]`. Unmarked prose, including every question, pattern, anti-pattern and the Worked Example scenario, is the distillation's own.
